Discharge Summary:

Patient Information: [redacted] Female, DOB [redacted], Hospital ID [redacted]. Admitted for chronic anicteric cholestasis and worsening cough with exertional dyspnea, diagnosed with chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome (BCS) complicating sarcoidosis. Histopathological findings confirmed BCS with liver, gastric, and skin biopsies. Patient received oral prednisolone and warfarin anticoagulation therapy and was discharged in stable condition.

Key Findings: The patient has diabetes mellitus evolving for 3 years without oral contraceptive use. Increased cholestatic enzymes (γ-glutamyl transferase 136 UI/L, alkaline phosphatase 325 UI/L) and normocytic inflammatory anemia with hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 82.8 fL, and serum ferritin 150 g/L were noted. Hepatomegaly with hypertrophied caudate lobe, splenomegaly, and portal hypertension were confirmed. Multinodular liver with absence of hepatic veins, centrolobular hepatocytes atrophy and fibrosis, and fibrosis were demonstrated. Mediastinal and hilar adenopathies with multiple micronodular opacities on lower pulmonary lobes were confirmed. Non-caseating granuloma on gastric biopsies and sarcoid granulomas on skin lesions were noted. ACE raised to 201 UECA, no tuberculin or bronchoalveolar lavage results.

Hospital Course: Patient started oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg and warfarin anticoagulation. Additional tests were performed to screen for prothrombotic disorder but failed to identify an underlying condition. BCS was the most likely diagnosis. Patient responded well and was discharged in stable condition.

Follow-up: Scheduled appointments with primary care and specialist providers. Patient and family advised to continue medications, monitor symptoms, and report concerns.

Chief Complaint: Profound hearing loss in the left ear, tinnitus, and dizziness  

Hospital Course: The patient was admitted in 2011 with profound hearing loss in the left ear and tinnitus, and dizziness. No nystagmus was noted during physical examination, and advanced vestibular tests were not conducted. Tonal audiometry showed a 37-dB hearing loss in the left ear with 70% speech discrimination, while the right ear showed normal pure tone audiometry. Radiological findings included a 4 mm diameter lesion in the internal auditory canal (IAC) associated with a left cerebellopontine angle (CPA) mass, which was confirmed as a CPA lipoma. The patient was followed up clinically and radiologically for two years without progression.  

Diagnosis: Left cerebellopontine angle (CPA) lipoma  

Discharge Instructions: The patient is advised to undergo routine follow-up with an otolaryngologist as per the physician's instructions. Follow-up imaging (CT/MRI) will be performed as prescribed.  

Signed, [Physician], MD

Discharge Summary:  
The patient, a 57-year-old male with extensive tobacco use, nonischemic cardiomyopathy, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status 3, received a mechanical cardiac support (LVAD) due to severe heart failure following successful initial evaluation. Three months post-surgery, a chest X-ray showed mediastinal widening and lymphadenopathy. CT scans confirmed lymphadenopathy outside the chest. A mediastinoscopy revealed consistent SCLC pathology. The patient was removed from active cardiac transplantation. Chemotherapy with carboplatin and IV etoposide was initiated while hospitalized. After his first cycle, the patient decided not to continue chemotherapy and opted for hospice care. Complications included cellulitis, pseudomonal neutropenia, and protracted nausea. The treatment course was complicated by prolonged IV antibiotic therapy, renal issues, and pleural and peripheral edema. The patient was discharged home and passed away approximately 6 months post-chemotherapy.

Admitted for carcinoma of the right breast with enlarged axillary lymph nodes, diagnosed as postradiogenic circumscribed scleroderma 20 months post radiation therapy. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy with anastrozole and abemaciclib was initiated as part of a clinical trial (NeoMONARCH). Adjuvant 3D conformal radiation therapy was delivered to the right breast and supraclavicular region.  

Radiation therapy resulted in moderate acute radiodermatitis with submammary moist epitheliolysis. A 2cm wide cutis edema at the irradiated area developed, which later expanded and caused inflammatory infiltrate, hyperpigmentation, and loss of breast volume. A targeted punch biopsy was performed to rule out lymphangiosis carcinomatosa cutis. Histology showed no malignant tumor, but dermal fibrosis and panniculitis were present with chronic perivascular inflammation.  

The patient was diagnosed with postradiogenic circumscribed scleroderma, and follow-up care is scheduled. She declined systemic immune suppression and opted for topical steroids and lymph drainage at a specialized center. Discharge instructions include scheduled checkups, monitoring affected areas, and sun protection.  

Discharge Diagnosis: Postradiogenic circumscribed scleroderma (morphea)  
Discharge Condition: Stable  
Discharge Medications: [None provided]  
Discharge Instructions: Check in with doctors for scheduled checkups, monitor affected areas, and apply sunscreen.

The patient, a 57-year-old female with a history of epilepsy, haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelet syndrome, sensorineural hearing loss, proteinuria, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and renal failure, was admitted for post-kidney transplantation follow-up. Upon admission, she reported visual symptoms related to a central scotoma. A thorough medical history revealed significant medical comorbidities, including IgA nephropathy, a mutation 4 years post-kidney transplant, and a m.3243A>G heteroplasmy in leucocytes. A kidney biopsy confirmed IgA nephropathy, necessitating peritoneal dialysis. A kidney transplant was performed at 52 years of age from a postmortem, heart-beating donor. Two years post-transplant, the patient developed left ventricle hypertrophy and diastolic heart failure, which remained stable. Four years post-transplantation, a m.3243A>G mutation was found with a heteroplasmy level of 6%. Discharge diagnosis includes IgA nephropathy, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and end-stage renal disease. The patient is currently stable with mild microalbuminuria, receiving prednisone and tacrolimus as immunosuppressants, and scheduled follow-up with her nephrologist.

The patient was admitted to the hospital due to multiple cervicofacial lacerations caused by a broken beer bottle. Upon admission, a suspected vascular injury was identified in the neck zone II. CT angiography revealed contrast leakage in the right internal carotid artery, and angiography via the right femoral artery showed extravasation in the neck zone III. A stent was inserted at the laceration site, and the patient underwent surgery to remove the hematoma and check for other injuries. The patient's condition improved, and follow-up observation and antiplatelet medication were prescribed. The patient is now discharged with no further injuries observed and has been advised to continue follow-up appointments.

**Hospital Course:**  
A 29-year-old white male farmer was admitted with left upper-quadrant abdominal discomfort and unintentional weight loss. Initial examination revealed splenomegaly, elevated leukocyte count, low hemoglobin, and high platelet count. Laboratory findings confirmed CML in chronic phase. Hydroxyurea was initiated, later substituted with imatinib. Splenomegaly resolved within 3 months, and the patient was re-evaluated at 3 months without symptoms. Imatinib was discontinued after 6 months due to pancytopenia. Bone marrow studies showed complete remission of CML and Leishmania amastigotes. Treatment with pentavalent antimonials was initiated, leading to complete recovery. Acute cardiac toxicity occurred, prompting suspension of treatment and replacement with amphotericin B. TKI therapy resumed after 3 months, with a PCR showing deep molecular response.  

**Diagnosis:** CML in chronic phase, pancytopenia, leishmaniasis, acute cardiac toxicity.  

**Summary:**  
The patient was diagnosed with CML in chronic phase and initiated imatinib. After a 6-month course, pancytopenia occurred, leading to discontinuation of imatinib. Leishmaniasis was treated with pentavalent antimonials, and TKI therapy resumed. The patient achieved complete molecular recovery and was discharged with follow-up care.

The patient presented with symptoms of burning, itching, pain, stinging, and decreased vision in her left eye, likely due to central keratitis and corneal scraping. She reported sand splash at the seaside and discontinued contact lens use ten days before admission. A biomicroscopic examination confirmed central keratitis and corneal scraping, with Acanthamoeba sp. cysts identified in the Giemsa-stained corneal scraping sample. The patient was treated with alternating topical fortified vancomycin, ceftazidime, propamidine isothionate 0.1%, and chlorhexidine at the clinic. Contact lenses and contact lens solution were not cultured. At the second visit, no growth was observed after inoculation of the corneal scraping specimen onto E. coli plates. The specimen was classified as a "T2" genotype "A. castellani" according to PCR and sequence analysis. The case was approved by the ethics committee at Uludag University Faculty of Medicine (2016-9/18), and informed consent was obtained from the patient.

Discharge Summary:  

The patient, [redacted], was admitted to the hospital with an eight-month history of generalized fatigue, increased thirst, urinary frequency and volume, reduced nocturnal erections, decreased sexual desire, and weight loss of 18 kg over six months. The patient was referred to endocrinology for evaluation of central diabetes insipidus and hypopituitarism. Initial findings included hypopituitarism, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, polyuria, and hypertonic hypernatremia, confirmed by MRI of the right-sided pituitary microadenoma. The patient was started on hydrocortisone and levothyroxine. Follow-up studies confirmed the initial diagnosis and ruled out autoimmune or inflammatory conditions. Tumor markers for germ cell tumors were negative, and a water deprivation test confirmed central diabetes insipidus. The patient was treated with testosterone replacement and desmopressin (DDAVP), along with a tissue biopsy confirming an intrasellar pituitary germinoma. A lumbar MRI scan and lumbar puncture were negative for metastasis. The patient was treated with whole ventricle brain radiation and showed improved clinical outcomes. The patient is scheduled for follow-up visits with the endocrinology clinic to monitor treatment and evaluate symptoms. Long-term follow-up is recommended for patients with intrasellar germinomas to monitor for recurrence or progression.

Discharge Summary:  
A male patient with a history of cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's-like symptoms was admitted to the hospital due to increasing memory decline and difficulty in daily functioning. He had no prior history of brain injury or neuropsychological disorders and no family history of dementia. Cognitive function was severely impaired, with abnormal levels of tau, p-tau, and Aβ1-42 in cerebrospinal fluid. A distinctively positive [C-11] Pittsburg compound B PET scan and [F-18] fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan with a typical AD-like hypometabolic pattern were performed. He was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. Treatment for cognitive impairment and AD-like symptoms was provided, and follow-up care was recommended for continued monitoring and management. The patient's family was advised to monitor and manage his condition with a primary care provider. Follow-up is scheduled with a primary care provider for continued care.

Discharge Summary: A 19-year-old female patient with pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma was admitted following surgical removal of the right adrenal tumor. The tumor was identified as pheochromocytoma and confirmed with occupying lesions in the left adrenal and paraganglion regions. Symptomatic findings included fever, headache, and hypertension. Additional scans revealed occupying lesions in the right lung and pancreas. The patient was treated with medications to manage symptoms, and further follow-up is recommended for monitoring of lesions. Discharge with continued follow-up for the combined tumor diagnosis.

A 17-year-old female patient with a history of orthodontic treatment resulting in an unfavorable outcome was referred after 31 months of orthodontic care. The patient underwent surgical orthodontic traction, resulting in significant bone loss distal to tooth 12 and mesial to tooth 14, with tooth 13 apex constrained within an ennis inverted Y. Periapical and panoramic radiographs showed bone loss and restricted tooth position. After proper orthodontic treatment, the patient opted for partial maxillary osteotomy. The procedure involved removal of the maxillary right canine and a partial osteotomy. Post-surgery, elastic traction was applied to complete the approximation, with intermaxillary immobilization for 21 days. A continuous arch-wire was used for stability and callus formation. Full orthodontic movements were cleared in April 2001, and full treatment concluded on October 2001. Removable retainers were installed. The patient requested the removal of internal fixation, which was done on October 29, 2010. Clinical and radiographic follow-up confirmed stability and pulpar vitality after 10 years and 10 months in January 2012.

The 87-year-old male was admitted to the emergency room with chest pain, light-headedness, and shortness of breath, which were exertional and left-sided, with a two-day duration. He reported no cough, fever, or infection, and was found to have muffled heart sounds and jugular venous distention. The patient has a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, recent pulseless ventricular tachycardia, and nonischemic cardiomyopathy. No further treatment information was provided. Follow-up is recommended for continued monitoring of cardiac stability and symptoms.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient: [REDACTED], Female, 54, Admitted for a sodium hydroxide splash injury of the left eye and symblepharon with superficial and deep corneal neovascularization. Discharge date: [REDACTED].  

Admitting diagnosis: Sodium hydroxide splash injury of left eye. Final diagnosis: Symblepharon with superficial and deep corneal neovascularization.  

Initial findings: A diffuse corneal epithelial defect, stromal edema, and Descemet’s folds were observed. Patient treated with 1% dexamethasone sodium phosphate drops, 1% atropine drops, and tobramycin. Prednisone 50mg, daily, was prescribed for ten days, followed by a 5mg tapering every 15 days.  

Follow-up: Subconjunctival bevacizumab (0.05ml, 1.25mg) was administered to the left eye. Patient was advised to use 0.3% ofloxacin and 1% dexamethasone sodium phosphate drops three times daily for one week after the first injection. A second injection was given two weeks later.  

Outcome: Visual acuity improved to 0.1 LogMAR two weeks post-injection, and corneal neovascularization was significantly reduced. The patient's condition was well-controlled. Follow-up 24 months later showed no change in VA and clinical status.

Discharge Summary:  
A 51-year-old male, a heavy smoker, was admitted with lymphadenopathy in the left neck, mediastinum, and a tubercle in the right lung. Pathological findings confirmed stage IV pulmonary adenocarcinoma. After four cycles of combination chemotherapy, 11 cycles of nimotuzumab, 12 cycles of maintenance pemetrexed, and 38 cycles of autologous lymphocyte reinfusion, the patient underwent mediastinal lymphadenectomy and wedge resection of the lower lobe of the right lung by video-assisted thoracic surgery. Post-surgery, the patient continued three cycles of combination chemotherapy. Subsequently, metastasis was detected in the central nervous system, and whole brain radiation therapy was administered. The patient remains completely asymptomatic, 31 months after pembrolizumab initiation, with no further follow-up plan specified. Condition at discharge: N/A. Discharge medications: N/A.

The patient was admitted with heart failure and a renal artery aneurysm and arteriovenous fistula. They were managed via endovascular occlusion, resulting in resolution of symptoms and improvement in renal function. Discharge instructions include follow-up with a primary care physician, adherence to medications, low-salt diet, and lifestyle modifications. The patient is advised to continue their current treatment plan and monitor renal and heart function as required.

Patient Information: Vietnamese, 55-year-old male, HBV cirrhosis without HDV, HCV or HIV coinfections, Grade 1 oesophageal varices. Diagnosis: 1997. Complication: oesophageal varices. 

Hospital Course: Patient was diagnosed with HBV cirrhosis without HDV, HCV or HIV coinfections in 1997, likely vertical transmission. Liver biopsy confirmed cirrhosis. Complicated by Grade 1 oesophageal varices and Child Pugh A score. 

In August 1998, started lamivudine at 100 mg/day. After 3 months, HBV-DNA undetectable by Digene assay. In 1999, undetectable by qualitative PCR. In 2000, lamivudine stopped due to HBV-DNA rise. Relapse detected with HBV-DNA 5.75 log10 and ALT 3.1 ULN. Continued treatment with adefovir dipivoxil for two years, HBV-DNA undetectable by quantitative PCR. 

In 2002, HBV-DNA detectable by PCR, viral breakthrough with HBV-DNA 9.2 log10. Asymptomatic. Sequenced mutations: rtL180M and rtM204V. Added adefovir and pegylated interferon, but treatment uneventful. In 2003, stopped lamivudine and adefovir; added adefovir. In 2004, HBV-DNA rose to 8.3 log10, ALT 10 ULN, and prothrombin time increased. Tenofovir fumarate started, adefovir continued, and treatment stopped. 

Overall, patient remains unremarkable. Liver transplantation planned as treatment of HBV cirrhosis.

The patient, a 2-day-old male newborn, was referred to us due to abnormal genitalia, imperforate anus, and distended bowel loops. Examination revealed a well-formed double penis with hypospadias, normal penile shaft, bifid scrotum, and a duplicated recto-sigmoid colon. The abdominal sonography showed distended bowel loops and normal kidneys. The patient underwent laparotomy, colostomy, and cystoplasty, leading to a diagnosis of Abnormal Genitalia with Double Penis and Hypospadias, Imperforate Anus with Distended and Duplicated Bowel Loops, and Duplicated Recto-Sigmoid Colon. He was successfully treated and discharged 2 weeks post-surgery. Follow-up instructions include regular monitoring, dietary guidelines, and communication with healthcare providers.

Discharge Summary  

The 40-year-old female patient, who had a history of ureteral stones, Behcet’s disease, and multiple myoma, was admitted for infertility treatment and underwent a laparoscopic-assisted myomectomy. Timed intercourse was initiated three months post-surgery. The patient was diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) based on an irregular menstrual cycle and elevated anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) levels. Standard treatment guidelines in Japan were followed, and the patient received cyclofenil (600 mg/d) for 5 days, starting on cycle day 5 until day 9, and chlormadinone acetate (4 mg/d) for 10 days, followed by clomiphene citrate (50 mg/day) for 5 days. A 48 × 41 mm anechoic mass was observed on the 11th day of the menstrual cycle, which was initially considered a follicle, but its clinical course indicated it to be a hyperovulatory corpus luteum (HOC). The mass disappeared on the 62nd day (19th day of the menstrual cycle), and the diagnosis was confirmed as a HOC. The patient was discharged in good health with no symptoms and a follow-up planned for her next routine visit.

Admitting Diagnosis: Paradoxical Reaction  
Hospital Course: The patient was referred to the department due to a new mass detected on chest CT during a routine checkup. A CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy confirmed caseating granulomas, leading to the diagnosis of paradoxical reaction. The patient was continued on anti-tuberculosis therapy, which was adjusted to isoniazid, rifapentine, and ethambutol due to liver damage. The size of the new pulmonary mass was reduced, and symptoms improved. The patient remains asymptomatic, with the original therapy continuing.

Patient: Female, 70, no prior breast health issues, no surgical history. Admitted for skin changes to left breast. Skin discoloration noted 6 months ago, progressing over time. Medical history includes hypertension, high cholesterol, diabetes, and osteoporosis. Patient denies symptoms like pain, mass, retraction, or lymphadenopathy. Vital signs and physical exam show no distress. Breast examination reveals a 3 × 3 cm pink, non-tender, raised lesion in the 12:00 position. Excisional biopsy confirmed primary cutaneous ALCL. No further treatment needed; patient recovering well. Follow-up with oncology. Discharged with ALCL diagnosis. Instructions: follow-up with oncology. Signed, [Physician Name], MD.

Discharge summary:  
A 70-year-old male with multiple comorbidities, including obstructive coronary artery disease, was admitted to the emergency department with chest pain and palpitations. Initial evaluation confirmed right ventricular outflow tract ventricular tachycardia (RVOT-VT), which was managed with external cardioversion. Subsequent treatment included intravenous amiodarone and further evaluation revealed left ventricular systolic dysfunction with a double chamber in the right ventricle. The patient was diagnosed with obstructive coronary artery disease several years ago, which was not treated. He experienced a brief episode of recurrent RVOT-VT, managed with another amiodarone loading dose. Surgical options such as resection of the muscular band, coronary artery bypass grafting, and subcutaneous ICD placement were explored, but he refused these options and was discharged home with a subcutaneous ICD in place.  

The patient was discharged on his prior medication regimen, including aspirin, atorvastatin, digoxin, lisinopril, and spironolactone-hydrochlorothiazide. Follow-up appointments were scheduled with his primary care physician and specialists as needed. The patient was advised to continue his medications and monitor symptoms, reporting any changes to his healthcare providers. He was discharged in stable condition and was instructed to follow up as scheduled.

The 22-year-old female of Indian origin was referred to the Department of Periodontics for persistent lip swelling and recurrent episodes of angular cheilitis. Hematological findings were consistent with microcytic hypochromic anemia, with low serum iron and folate levels, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. A biopsy was performed to rule out intestinal involvement, and Mantoux and Kveim tests ruled out active tubercular infection and sarcoidosis. The diagnosis was oral Crohn's disease without intestinal manifestations. Treatment included anti-inflammatory drugs and corticosteroid supplements, with topical steroid applications for oral ulcerations and vitamin supplements for angular cheilitis. External gingivectomy was planned after extensive oral prophylaxis and subgingival scaling. Follow-up revealed no gastrointestinal symptoms, and hematological tests showed no significant changes. While oral ulcerations and lip swelling improved, the gingiva remained normal. The patient is expected to follow up for 15 months.

Discharge Summary:  
The patient was admitted to the hospital with difficulty flushing a PEG tube and localized PEG-tube site pain. An external bulge was identified at the gastrostomy site, and the PEG tube appeared to have migrated. BBS was suspected. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a bulge at the fistula site with an internal bumper embedded within the gastric lumen. After external traction, the buried PEG tube was removed without complications. A 14 F, 1.7-cm Mic-Key® button was placed over the guidewire, and kidney, ureter, and bladder X-rays were performed, showing no free air. The patient was discharged home without further complications. Diagnosis: difficulty flushing the PEG tube and localized PEG-tube pain. Treatment: external traction, PEG tube removal, and placement of the Mic-Key button. Follow-up: no further hospital follow-up was required. Discharge medications: none prescribed. Discharge condition: stable and uncomplicated.

A 6-year-old female patient with left-sided CMT and a right-sided chest wall mass was admitted for evaluation. A persistent dry cough and incidental chest wall mass were noted, with no known predisposing factors. Physical examination revealed left-sided torticollis and a firm mass at the level of the fourth to sixth ribs on the right side, confirmed by a chest skiogram and CT. The tumor involved the right upper zone, and a postoperative thoracotomy was performed with tumor excision, removal of the left SCM tendon, and partial removal of the fifth rib. Histopathology confirmed a desmoid tumor with negative margins. The patient will be closely monitored for recurrence and follow-up with oncology. No medications were prescribed, and follow-up is scheduled for oncology. Conditions on discharge: Desmoid tumor.

Admitting Diagnosis: Chronic pain syndrome with failed back surgery syndrome (FBSS)  

The patient presented with a long-standing history of intractable chronic pain in both lower back and legs, despite multiple surgical and non-surgical interventions, including 14 spinal surgeries, block injections, and medications. A mixed pain syndrome was identified, consisting of a neuropathic radicular component in both legs and a nociceptive component in the lower back. Initial spinal cord stimulation (SCS) provided excellent bilateral pain relief for the legs but not for the axial lower back pain. Subsequent deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the periaqueductal gray (PVG) on the nondominant side achieved excellent axial spinal pain relief.  

During the 22 years of follow-up, combined SCS/PVG stimulation maintained complete relief of pain in both lower back and leg regions, with electrode programming adjustments made after accidental exposure to magnetic fields or battery depletion. Wire-connector revisions were required after motor vehicle accidents. The patient’s chronic pain condition has been fully controlled with the neuromodulation intervention for the past 22 years, with complete pain relief and return to normal life.  

Follow-Up Care: The patient will continue to follow up with the neurosurgical pain clinic for regular reprogramming visits and maintenance of the neuromodulation systems.  

Signed, [insert name of physician]

A 76-year-old man with exertional dyspnea, visual disturbances, night sweats, and progressive fatigue was admitted. He had a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol, and alcohol abuse. On physical examination, petechiae and hematoma were noted on the lower extremities, with no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Laboratory findings showed an extremely elevated white blood cell count (220 × 10⁹/L), low hemoglobin, and low platelet count. A peripheral blood smear revealed a high proportion of blasts and promyelocytes, indicating acute myeloproliferative disorder (APL) with potential for leukemia. Other findings included elevated LDH and creatinine levels. The patient was treated with leukapheresis in addition to chemotherapy and ATRA. The diagnosis was confirmed, and the patient was discharged with appropriate instructions for follow-up.

A 67-year-old Hispanic male was admitted with generalized body weakness, difficulty sleeping, abdominal pain, increased thirst, and constipation. The diagnosis was a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with squamous features suggestive of pancreaticobiliary primary. Cisplatin and gemcitabine were initiated, but the patient experienced recurrent admissions with worsening symptoms and uncontrolled hypercalcemia. His condition was further complicated by acute kidney injury, cholestatic hyperbilirubinemia, and pancreatitis, necessitating percutaneous transhepatic cholecystostomy (PTC). The patient ultimately expired within three months of his diagnosis.

Patient: Case 8, 30-year-old female  
Chief Complaint: Elevated CK, episodes of palpitation  

Discharge Summary: The patient was admitted for evaluation of elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels and palpitations. Initial ECG showed T wave inversion and normal transthoracic echocardiography. Genetic testing (next-generation sequencing) revealed a heterozygous carrier of a missense variant in the COL6A1 gene (c. 1273-4T>C) with unknown significance. Patient remained stable and was monitored overnight. Cardiology team recommended outpatient follow-up with ECG monitoring, Holter monitoring, and exercise stress testing. Follow-up instructions include continued use of systemic lupus erythematosus medications, regular follow-up with primary care, and scheduling of a cardiology appointment for palpitation monitoring. Genetic counseling was recommended to assess the VUS variant's impact. Orthopedic follow-up is advised for myalgia symptoms. Patient is discharged in stable condition.

Brief Hospital Course: A 29-year-old female medical microbiologist in training was admitted to our hospital with symptoms of low-grade fever, general malaise, and a retro-orbital headache following a trip to Suriname. She was bitten by mosquitos during her visit and developed a non-itching maculopapular rash on her trunk and extremities, along with slight conjunctival injection. Stiffness and edema were noted in her wrists, knees, and ankles, and she experienced contact lens intolerance. Her condition improved after 7 days of observation, and she was discharged home in stable condition.  

Diagnostic Assessment: Urine and plasma testing confirmed a diagnosis of ZIKV infection, with positive results for RNA and virus culture. No infectious virus was recovered.  

Summary of Events: The patient was diagnosed with ZIKV infection after returning from a trip to Suriname, where she was bitten by mosquitoes. She presented with symptoms consistent with the disease and was discharged after 7 days of observation.  

Follow-Up: Follow-up instructions were provided for any future symptoms or concerns, with further management deferred. Discharged home in stable condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Patient Name]  
MR#: [Medical Record Number]

Hospitals Course:  
A 62-year-old male with a history of tobacco abuse and newly diagnosed small-cell lung cancer was readmitted to the hospital with shortness of breath. He had been on chemotherapy and radiation for his cancer over the previous month and was treated for acute idiopathic pericarditis, which was initiated on four days prior.

Admission Findings:  
Upon admission, the patient had a temperature and was slightly hypoxic. Jugular venous distension was noted without Kussmaul's sign or pulsus paradoxus. Laboratory results showed reduced white blood cell and neutrophil counts, elevated creatinine and blood urea nitrogen levels, and high lactic acid levels. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed normal voltage, but diffuse ST-segment elevations were observed. Urgent transthoracic echocardiography revealed large pericardial effusion causing tamponade and right ventricular collapse in diastole, with a dilated inferior vena cava. Emergency pericardiocentesis was performed, and 800 mL of green fluid was drained.

Treatment and Outcome:  
The patient was diagnosed with purulent pericarditis and treated with intravenous ertapenem based on microbial cultures. A partial pericardiectomy and sepsis resolved. The source of the polymicrobial pericarditis was unclear, but a CT scan and chest imaging confirmed no recurrence of pericardial effusion. The patient was discharged home on day 8 of hospitalization. Continued chemo-radiation therapy was initiated 2 months post-discharge. No recurrence of pericardial effusion was observed following a TTE 4 weeks post-discharge.

Chief Complaint: Invasive low-grade carcinoma of the appendix colonizing appendicial endometriosis.  

History: A 45-year-old female was admitted for a second laparotomy and HIPEC following a previous diagnosis of acute appendicitis and multiple peritoneal mucinous implants in the right pelvis. She underwent a right hemicolectomy, omentectomy, bilateral ovariectomy, and peritoneal resections with HIPEC. Pathology revealed foci of endometriosis on the ileal surface of the right hemicolectomy, the left Fallopian tube, and in one of the peritoneal fragments. Free intrabdominal mucin was absent, and acellular mucin was localized on the right peritoneal surface. Both ovaries had functional cysts.  

Diagnosis: Invasive low-grade carcinoma of the appendix colonizing appendicial endometriosis.

The patient, diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) at an outside hospital, underwent induction chemotherapy, double-delayed intensification, and maintenance therapy. He experienced a CNS relapse after 15 months, treated with the same protocol along with whole brain and whole spine irradiation. Four months post-remission, he developed a second relapse with ≥90% leukemic blasts in the bone marrow, which was treated with aggressive reinduction chemotherapy. The patient died 3 months after the second relapse, with no response to the treatment. The follow-up indicates that the patient's disease progression and treatment outcome were not fully responsive. The patient, a 74-year-old male, presented with repeated cough, expectoration, and wheezing over 8 years. Chest pain and shortness of breath were observed for 7 days. Upon admission, bronchoscopy revealed right middle lobe obstruction, with acid-fast bacilli negative on biopsy. Chest X-ray showed atelectasis, and the initial diagnosis was chronic bronchitis and bronchial anthracofibrosis. The patient was discharged after treatment of an exacerbation.  

The patient returned to the hospital 9 months later with chest pain and progressive shortness of breath. Physical examination revealed dullness to percussion and disappearance of right lower lung breath sounds. Chest CT showed right pleural effusion, with multiple white nodules on parietal pleura. A biopsy confirmed granulomatous inflammation, and the diagnosis was revised to tuberculous pleuritis. Anti-tuberculosis treatment reduced pleural effusion and resolved symptoms. The patient was discharged in stable condition with follow-up to primary care and continued treatment.

Patient, 36-year-old male, with Wilson's disease, admitted with deciduous teeth affected by generalized gingivitis and multiple moderate-to-advanced dental caries. Admitted for operative, periodontal, and prosthodontic treatments. Due to his mental retardation and fear of dental procedures, the treatments were performed under general anesthesia in two minimal visits. During the procedures, electrocardiography, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, end-tidal capnography, body temperature, and entropy levels were monitored. An IV line was secured with O2 and N2O gases, and 4% sevoflurane and atracurium were administered. The patient was intubated with a 26-mm endotracheal tube. Anesthesia was maintained with O2 and N2O gases and 2% sevoflurane. State entropy (SE) and response entropy (RE) were maintained in the range of 30–45 and 35–54, respectively. No specific events occurred. The patient received various operative, periodontal, and prosthodontic treatments, including scaling, composite filling, inlay preparation, gold crown preparation, simple extraction, and caries treatment. During the try-in step, a gold crown slid from the surgeon's hand and was incidentally found near the endotracheal tube balloon. The prosthesis was removed using video-assisted laryngoscopy and curvilinear forceps. Dental floss-tied gauze packing was performed. No complications were experienced. The patient was discharged 1 hour after stabilization. Discharge diagnosis: Decayed teeth with generalized gingivitis and multiple moderate-to-advanced dental caries. Discharge condition: Stable with no complications. Discharge plan: Patient is instructed to maintain routine medication and follow-up with primary care physician. He is advised to maintain good oral hygiene and attend regular dental check-ups. Postoperative instructions include incision care, activity, diet, and medication use. Patient and guardian were fully informed of all aspects of discharge and the need to seek immediate medical attention if necessary. Follow-up appointments: Primary care physician and regular dental check-ups.

A 60-year-old female presented with shortness of breath, palpitation, chest pain, and progressive dyspnea. She had a history of dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea. Physical examination revealed arterial blood pressure of 135/90 mmHg, heart rate of 110 bpm, SpO₂ 94%, and respiratory rate of 24 bpm. No significant medical history was noted. Diagnostic testing showed normal cardiac enzymes, biochemical analysis, and complete blood count except for elevated eosinophilia. Chest radiography revealed cardiomegaly with a bulging left heart border, and ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with poor R wave progression and no ST segment changes. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a large multicystic mass extending from the left ventricle lateral wall to the pericardium, causing pressure effects on the left ventricle. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a well-defined, thin-walled, homogeneous multiple cardiac hydatid cyst with internal trabeculae. A serologic test for hydatidosis was positive, and the patient had elevated eosinophilia. After diagnosis, the cyst was surgically excised, and postoperative management included intercostal block, tramadol, and diclofenac sodium. The patient was extubated and had a normal hemodynamic status. The patient's recovery was uneventful, and she was discharged with no restrictions, with a follow-up recommendation for further management.

**Final Diagnosis**:  
- Streptococcus salivarius meningitis  
- Antiphospholipid syndrome  
- Cerebrospinal fluid leak (CSF-L)  
- Ventriculitis  
- Encephalopathy  

**Hospital Course**:  
The patient was admitted with acute worsening of headache, new-onset neck and back pain, photophobia, and pain exacerbated by spine flexion. Laboratory findings included cloudy CSF, glucose <10 mg/dL, protein 732 mg/dL, and nucleated cells 2764/uL with 87% segmented neutrophils. CSF Gram-positive cocci were found, and culture of CSF grew Streptococcus salivarius. IV therapy with dexamethasone, cefepime, and vancomycin was initiated. Bilateral endoscopic ethmoid repair and lumbar drain placement were performed. Post-repair re-leak and ventriculitis developed, necessitating additional intrathecal antibiotics and a ventriculo-peritoneal shunt. CSF studies cleared, and ventriculostomy placement was completed.  

**Follow-up Recommendations**:  
- Follow up with primary care provider for antiphospholipid syndrome and CSF-L monitoring  
- Continue apixaban as prescribed and monitor for bleeding  
- Follow up with otolaryngologist and neurosurgery  
- Complete full course of antibiotics

The patient is discharged with a plan to follow up with care providers and specialists. Antibiotics are prescribed and continued as needed. The patient is advised to monitor for bleeding and follow up as required. Education on medication compliance and follow-up care is provided.

A routine hemogram showed pancytopenia with a total leukocyte count of 3000/μL and a platelet count of 20,000/μL. A bone marrow trephine biopsy revealed partial replacement of normal marrow with blasts, megakaryocytes with multinucleation, and negative staining for myeloperoxidase and leukocyte common antigen. A 25-year-old gravida 3, para 2002 at 32 0/7 weeks' gestation, was admitted with intermittent severe abdominal pain and obstipation. She had a history of hypothyroidism, microcytic anemia, and sigmoid volvulus in her prior pregnancy. On physical examination, suprapubic and right lower quadrant tenderness were noted, with normal bowel sounds. A nonanomalous singleton fetus was confirmed via ultrasound. Abdominal radiography showed colonic distention, and laboratory evaluation was unremarkable. Colonoscopic decompression was performed with rectal tube placement for 24 hours, followed by a second decompression during the second week. At 38 1/7 weeks, a third decompression was performed, leading to a spontaneous vaginal delivery. Postpartum complications included worsening abdominal pain and a recurrence of sigmoid distention with a history of volvulus. A fourth decompression was performed, and the patient was discharged home. Follow-up included a fifth decompression and a laparoscopic sigmoidectomy. Histopathologic evaluation confirmed benign findings, and the patient is currently monitored for recurrence.

A 46-year-old male patient was admitted with complaints of pain and swelling in the maxillary anterior region of the jaw. He had previously undergone endodontic treatment for the affected teeth, which initially improved the symptoms. However, the swelling gradually increased and was accompanied by dull, throbbing pain from 1 month prior to the visit. Diagnostic findings revealed a solitary diffused extraoral swelling in the upper anterior region of the face, a well-defined swelling in the maxillary anterior labial vestibule, and a tender, fluctuant lesion. The patient also exhibited a deviated nasal tip and elevated left nasolabial fold. Radiographic findings showed a large, well-defined, corticated periapical radiolucency along with an impacted mesiodens, along with a dilacerated supernumerary tooth. The patient was diagnosed with an infected dentigerous cyst and surgically removed along with the impacted mesiodens. Postoperatively, the patient's complaints of pain and swelling in the maxillary anterior region resolved, and he was discharged with oral hygiene instructions and follow-up visits with a dental care provider.

Patient: 70-year-old male with a fractured neck of the femur of the right hip secondary to age-related osteoporosis.  
Hospital Course: Presented with hip pain, swelling, and restricted mobility following a fall at home. Radiographic and clinical findings revealed a fractured femoral head-neck junction, diagnosed via X-ray and bone density studies. Postoperative treatment included a posterior hemi-replacement arthroplasty with a cemented bipolar prosthesis. On day 5 post-surgery, the patient experienced right hip clicking while walking.  

The patient was readmitted for reassessment of the surgical outcome. Radiographs showed no open wound, no dilated veins, and no neurological deficits. Palpation revealed tenderness over the right Scarpa's area with bitrochanteric compression test positive. No complications were noted. Open reduction and fixation were performed through the old surgical scar. The femoral head component was fully incorporated into the acetabulum, with no defects or scratches. The prosthesis was removed, and a post-operative X-ray of the pelvis shows a new femoral head with a longer offset.  

Outcome: Patient is currently asymptomatic and has a favorable outcome. Follow-up is scheduled for 1 year.

A 91-year-old Japanese woman with a history of acute-onset type 1 diabetes and absolute insulin deficiency was admitted with post-meal blood glucose levels of 252 mg/dl and an HbA1c level of 9.6%. The patient's therapeutic regimen included premixed biphasic insulin aspart, miglitol, and aliskiren. Sitagliptin (25 mg/day) was added to better control diabetes, resulting in occasional mild hypoglycemia, glucose drinks, and a reduction in HbA1c levels from 9.6% to 7.4%. Aliskiren was replaced with candesartan due to rising blood pressure. Post-meal C-peptide levels remained undetectable (below 0.1 ng/ml) after sitagliptin treatment. No adverse events were observed in kidney, liver, or gastrointestinal function, and no gastrointestinal complaints or weight gain were noted. Follow-up included no special differences in diet management or physical exercise before and during sitagliptin treatment.

The patient, a 40-year-old female, was admitted with suspected organophosphorus poisoning, presenting with acute abdominal pain, vomiting, and altered mental status. Initial investigations showed normal serum electrolytes and blood gas analysis, but a strong suspicion of organophosphorus poisoning led to treatment with atropine and parenteral hydration. The patient's condition improved over 12 hours, with a partial recovery. On day 7, delayed onset intermediate syndrome developed, requiring intensified treatment with atropine and pralidoxime. The patient was discharged on day 22, with full recovery noted on a 6-week follow-up. The clinical findings included bilateral constricted pupils, muscle fasciculations, and normal organomegaly. The patient, a 38-year-old female, was discharged with a diagnosis of recurrent ductal carcinoma in situ (RDCIS) of the breast, requiring a total mastectomy with immediate reconstruction using a DIEP flap. She opted for a DIEP flap due to her active runner's lifestyle. The procedure involved a stacked DIEP flap with two single perforators on each hemi-abdomen, using two sets of deep inferior epigastric vessels. A single set was anastomosed to the antegrade internal mammary vessels, while the other set was anastomosed to the retrograde internal mammary vessels. The flap was folded and inset for optimal volume and projection. The patient had a satisfactory aesthetic outcome with no fat necrosis and a computed tomographic (CT) angiogram of the chest performed incidentally on postoperative day 5, which revealed patent vascular anastomoses to both pedicles. A one-year follow-up was scheduled with her surgeon, and the patient reported a satisfactory aesthetic outcome with no complications.

A 85-year-old Japanese woman with Stage IV squamous cell lung cancer was admitted eight days post-pembrolizumab monotherapy, presenting with rapidly worsening general fatigue and appetite loss. She had been previously diagnosed with Stage IV cancer seven months prior, and pembrolizumab was the first-line therapy. Routine examination before each infusion revealed no significant changes. Physical examination showed no abnormalities. Laboratory findings included low serum cortisol, inappropriately low ACTH, hyponatremia with elevated ADH, and hypoglycemia. Urine osmolarity was abnormal despite normal plasma osmolarity, indicating inappropriate ADH secretion. Standard-dose ACTH testing did not show a response. Serum anti-pituitary cell antibody-1 was negative. The patient was diagnosed with isolated ACTH deficiency. Hydrocortisone administration improved the patient's condition, corrected ADH levels, normalized sodium, and restored glucose. The adrenal glands were unremarkable on CT. Discharged with follow-up care. Follow-up showed persistent ACTH deficiency and normal thyroid function, with no abnormalities in white blood cells, eosinophils, or glucose.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient [REDACTED], a 35-year-old female, was admitted for worsening headaches and was treated with propranolol and flunarazine. She was discharged. One month later, she was readmitted with persistent headaches and acute onset blurring of vision. An ophthalmological examination revealed bilateral refractive errors of -0.5 diopters, and topiramate was prescribed for two weeks. Visual symptoms persisted, and the diagnosis was suspected to be topiramate-induced acute myopia. The medication was discontinued, and she was referred to the ophthalmologist, where her refractive error worsened to -3.5 diopters bilaterally. The patient was discharged with no complaints. Follow-up appointments with her general practitioner and ophthalmologist were arranged, and she was instructed not to take topiramate again. The patient's condition improved significantly, and no further treatment was needed.

Patient Name: [redacted]  
Medical Record Number: [redacted]  
Date of Admission: [redacted]  
Date of Discharge: [redacted]  

Admission Diagnosis: Epigastric pain, vomiting  
Discharge Diagnosis: Symptomatic cystic lymphangioma originating from the left adrenal gland  

Hospital Course: The patient was admitted with persistent epigastric pain and vomiting, which were not related to food intake. An ultrasonography and CT scan revealed a retroperitoneal cystic mass on the left side. A CT-guided puncture was performed, but the cyst was not evacuated due to technical issues. Cytology showed no malignant cells, and the diagnosis was compatible with a cystic lymphangioma. To assess the location of the cyst more precisely, a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed, which confirmed a cystic lymphangioma originating from the left adrenal gland. A surgical resection was proposed due to persistent pain. During surgery, an "en bloc" left adrenalectomy was performed without rupture of the cyst. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 5.  

Follow-up: The patient was seen at the outpatient clinic one month after the surgery and reported no further symptoms. The final diagnosis was confirmed by histopathology and immunohistochemistry.  

Differential Diagnosis: Primary adrenal tumors, metastatic adenocarcinomas, angiosarcomas, multicystic mesotheliomas, or adrenal cysts were considered.  

Treatment: Surgical resection is the definitive treatment for symptomatic cystic lymphangioma. Complete resection of the cyst is recommended, and associated parenchymal resection (adrenalectomy) depends on the cyst's location and intraoperative dissection.  

Discharge Condition: The patient was discharged in stable condition and instructed to follow up as an outpatient.  

Follow-up Plan: The patient was advised to return to the outpatient clinic for follow-up consultations.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient [Redacted] was discharged on [Redacted] with instructions to follow a proper diet and continue regular follow-up appointments. The patient, diagnosed with Gross Hydronephrosis (GH) caused by a kidney stone at the junction of the ureter and renal pelvis, was admitted for further evaluation. Key findings included a longitudinal surgical scar on the upper abdomen and a mass on the left side of the abdomen. The hospital course revealed a massive hypoechoic lesion occupying almost the entire abdomen, with adhesion between the kidney and surrounding organs. A complete nephrectomy and removal of the affected kidney were performed, resulting in long-lasting hiccups and improvement in appetite and overall health. The patient was discharged with no recurrence of hiccups and no further complications. Follow-up appointments are recommended.

Discharge Summary:

The patient, a 18-month-old female, was admitted with mild fever and intermittent sinus discharge in the mid-dorsal area. She underwent a dorsal D1 to D8 laminectomy, mid-line myelotomy, and total tumor excision under microscope. Intra-operative and post-operative methylprednisolone doses were administered. On post-operative day 10, she developed mild weakness in the left lower limb, which was resolved. Histopathological findings confirmed a dermoid cyst. The cyst was identified as T1-weighted (T1W) hypointense, T2-weighted (T2W) and short tau inversion recovery (STIR) hyperintense, restricted diffusion in diffusion-weighted (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) images, with no fat signal. A tuft of hair and a capsule were removed, and the dermal sinus tract was excised. Dural closure was performed, and the patient is discharged with follow-up.

A 41-year-old male with a history of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma presented with acute gastrointestinal bleeding in September 2004. He was treated with three cycles of R-CHOP chemotherapy, but no response was observed. After a surgical procedure, a retroperitoneal lymph node biopsy confirmed an infiltrative carcinoma, with immunohistochemical analysis showing chromogranin and synaptophysin expression and Ki-67 < 3%. Family History: Prostate cancer and lymphoma/leukemia in family members.  

Physical Exam: No neurofibromatosis cutaneous stoma, but thoracic and abdominal neurofibromas were noted.  

Diagnosis: Low-grade neuroendocrine tumor, CLL, and marginal zone B-cell lymphoma/chronic lymphocytic leukemia.  

Treatment: Octreotide acetate until recovery, followed by R-CHOP and CHOP cycles. CLL is currently under clinical surveillance. The patient is out of treatment.  

Follow-Up: Monitor CLL and any future medical concerns.

Patient is a 10-year-old female with known 22q11DS, cardiac anomalies, conductive hearing loss, malformed ossicular chain, and narrow ear canals. Tympanostomy tube placement was done at age 3, and she wears hearing aids since age 4.  

Middle ear inspection and ossicular reconstruction (left side) were performed due to conductive hearing loss and difficulty in wearing hearing aids. CT scan pre-op showed epitympanic ossicular fixation and a more horizontal orientation of the incus and dehiscent facial nerve canal on the left side. A retroauricular incision was performed, and the external auditory canal was widened and saucerized. Curetting of the epitympanic fixation of the malleus and removal of the anteriorly fixed manubrium resulted in a mobile ossicular chain. Audiometry tests showed improved hearing at frequencies 0.25, 5, 1, and 2 kHz.  

No complications were reported. Follow-up is advised with the otorhinolaryngologic department and regular audiology testing.  

Diagnoses: 22q11DS, cardiac anomalies, conductive hearing loss, malformed ossicular chain, narrow ear canals, epitympanic ossicular fixation, more horizontal incus orientation, dehiscent facial nerve canal.  

Procedures: Tympanostomy tube placement, middle ear inspection and ossicular reconstruction.

A 65-year-old male with diabetes, hypertension, and spinal cord injury presented with high fever on postoperative day 10 following partial lung resection for adenocarcinoma. CT scan revealed empyema, and Streptococcus caprae was detected by wound culture. The patient underwent irrigation, thoracic drainage, and broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment for 16 days. Although the infection reduced in size, it remained active. On postoperative day 36, non-open wound therapy with Negative Pressure Wound Therapy (NPWTi-d) was initiated, and the patient continued treatment for 20 days until the infection was resolved. Four months later, no empyema recurrence was observed, and the patient was discharged with follow-up care. The multidisciplinary team provided appropriate care, resulting in successful treatment and no further complications.

Discharge Summary:  
A five-year-old female cousin of Case-2 was admitted with minimal skin lesions and abnormal gait, but normal intelligence. A radiographic study was conducted, revealing abnormal craniofacial contours (Case-2) with total sagittal suture synostosis and mild plagiocephaly. Case-1 exhibited brachycephaly and partial coronal/lambdoid synostosis, while Case-2 showed scaphocephaly and sagittal suture synostosis. CT scans of the skull and spine demonstrated severe osteolysis in the shoulders and hips, and a "shepherd's crook" deformity in the pelvis. The patient underwent a comprehensive radiographic study, and further diagnostic and therapeutic interventions are recommended.

Patient Name: Anonymous

Date of Discharge: Ongoing  

Admission Diagnosis: Squamous cell carcinoma  

Hospital Course Summary:  
The 81-year-old Japanese male patient was admitted with a chief complaint of pain in the right lingual margin due to a mass. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed an enhanced soft tissue mass at the right lingual margin. A biopsy confirmed squamous cell carcinoma, and tumor resection was performed under general anesthesia.  

After eight months, follow-up CT showed a swelling in the right upper cervical region. A RND was performed according to traditional method, and adjuvant chemotherapy was planned but discontinued due to poor physical condition. Six months post-RND, a pathologic fracture with bone destruction was detected. A PET-CT confirmed low tumor metastasis probability. US on October 5, 2010, showed a clavicle fracture likely due to non-neoplastic changes.  

Follow-up CT scans were conducted over six years, with no signs of recurrence or metastasis. The patient continues to undergo regular follow-up CT scans to monitor the clavicle fracture and ensure no recurrence of the malignant tumor.  

Discharge Condition: Stable, with no signs of recurrence or metastasis detected.  

Recommendations: Continue regular follow-up CT scans to monitor the clavicle fracture and ensure no recurrence of the malignant tumor.

Admission Summary: The patient presented to the outpatient clinic with left knee pain, which had progressed over several months, leading to a painful left hip and an antalgic gait. No abnormalities were observed on inspection, but the patient experienced a gait disturbance, with the left knee consistently kept straight during gait. A full range of motion was noted, but flexion of the knee caused pain. Swelling was palpable at the lateral side of the left knee joint.

Hospital Course Summary: Radiographs and MRI confirmed calcification of the lateral region of the cartilaginous epiphysis of both the distal femoral and proximal tibia of the left knee, with evidence of epiphyseal overgrowth. A surgical resection of the lateral femoral epicondyle was performed, which removed the cartilage overgrowth and reduced swelling. The tibial plateau was not resected, but the patient was advised to continue monitoring for further complications.

Discharge Summary: The patient was discharged in satisfactory condition. No post-operative complications were reported. History of Present Illness: The patient, a 53-year-old male, presented with upper abdominal discomfort and meteorism, accompanied by vomiting, which occurred approximately two hours after meals and lasted for hours. The symptoms resolved within a few hours, and the initial diagnosis was biliary colic and dyspepsia.

Hospital Course: Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a pseudo kidney image in the transverse colon, and abdominal tomography showed a 9 cm segment of diffuse thickening along the transverse colon wall, along with colocolic intussusception. Endoscopic examination confirmed an intraluminal fatty lesion causing nonnecrotizing intussusception in the distal transverse colon. The patient underwent a left hemicolectomy with end-to-end anastomosis. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on his sixth postoperative day.

Diagnostic Assessment: Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed a lipomatous lesion of 5 cm diameter in the transverse colon, with no signs of malignancy. Histopathologic examination confirmed a benign, lipomatous lesion.

Condition at Discharge: The patient was discharged in stable condition, with instructions on wound care and symptom management.

Follow-Up Instructions: The patient was advised to contact his primary care physician for any concerns or questions. He was to schedule a follow-up appointment with the surgeon within four weeks post-discharge to monitor the surgical site and assess any further symptoms.

The patient, a 23-year-old male with a history of biliary cirrhosis and recent episodic abdominal pain, was admitted with abdominal pain and jaundice. Abdominal CT revealed hepatosplenomegaly with collateral vessels and esophageal varices. Esophageal varices were identified via endoscopy, and blood tests showed elevated bilirubin, aspartate aminotransferase, and alanine aminotransferase levels. The patient also had elevated levels of coproporphyrin in stool and uroporphyrin in urine. Due to acute liver failure and intra-abdominal bleeding causing hypovolemic shock, the patient was scheduled for an emergency liver transplant. The procedure was successful, but post-transplant complications, including severe sensory and motor polyneuropathy, occurred. Despite antibiotic administration and improved liver function tests, the patient developed multi-organ failure and expired on post-operative day 104.

Discharge Summary  
A 72-year-old man with well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) for Brugada syndrome was admitted to the hospital with fever and left upper extremity seizure. CT scans confirmed asymptomatic chronic subdural hematoma, which remained unchanged over 2 years. The patient was negative for human immunodeficiency virus and not immunocompromised.  

The patient underwent a craniotomy under general anesthesia. Post-operative findings included a thickened, hardened, and yellowish outer membrane of the subdural hematoma capsule, with pus collected. The inferior component of the subdural hematoma was organized, and the inner membrane strongly adhered to the cerebral cortex. The hematomas were not removed to prevent infection spread. The definitive diagnosis was intracranial subdural empyema with organized chronic subdural hematoma.  

Histopathological analysis revealed fibrous hypertrophy and inflammatory changes in the outer membrane. Drainage and antibiotic intravenous therapy (4 weeks) were initiated, leading to normal serum CRP levels. The patient was discharged with oral minocycline (200 mg every 12 hours) and continued to follow up with a primary care physician for wound healing and diabetes management. The patient was advised to continue the medication for the recommended duration.

The patient was a preterm baby delivered vaginally at 34 weeks gestation with gross anomalies including narrow chest indicating lung hypoplasia, fused lower limbs and feet with 10 toes, absence of external genitalia, imperforate anus, and single umbilical artery. Investigation revealed the presence of diabetes mellitus in the mother. Despite aggressive medical management, the patient died due to severe respiratory distress. On autopsy, there was observable bilateral renal agenesis, two pea-sized gonads suggesting bilateral posterior testes, and disruptions in the gastrointestinal tract. The findings indicate a preterm birth with significant congenital anomalies, leading to a life-threatening condition. The patient's death was attributed to respiratory distress, and follow-up is recommended for further evaluation of renal and gonadal function.

The patient, a 35-year-old male, was admitted with progressive memory impairment, left hemiparesis, and language disorder, presenting with a history of arterial hypertension, left total hip replacement for avascular necrosis, and chronic convulsive syndrome. A brain biopsy revealed necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis, which was confirmed by MRI. Autoimmune, infectious, and malignant diseases were ruled out, and treatment with cyclophosphamide and methylprednisolone was initiated. The patient returned to the hospital two years later with aggressive behavior, mutism, incontinence, and progressive neurological deterioration, which were further documented on a new brain MRI showing two frontoparietal and left cerebellar inflammatory lesions consistent with the progression of the vasculitis. Despite treatment with methylprednisolone and rituximab, the patient's condition continued to deteriorate, and he ultimately passed away. The patient had a history of multiple medical conditions and presented with neurological symptoms. After a brain biopsy, he was diagnosed with necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis and received various treatments, but the disease progression led to his death.

Discharge Summary:  
A 68-year-old female, with a medical history of metastatic melanoma, hypertension, deep vein thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism, was admitted with altered mental status, hypotension, and fever. She had recently received her second dose of immunotherapy with ipilimumab and nivolumab. Upon admission, vital signs included a blood pressure of 75/40 mm Hg, heart rate 110 bpm, respiratory rate 24 bpm, oxygen saturation 95%, and temperature 98.4°C. Physical examination revealed altered mental status, moderate respiratory distress, and bilateral lower extremity edema. Initial blood work showed elevated white blood cells, platelets, and other metabolic parameters.  

The patient was managed for sepsis with multiorgan failure in the context of an RTA (Immunotherapy-Related Thrombocytopenia). A differential diagnosis of sepsis, adrenal insufficiency, antimicrobial toxicity, and immunotherapy adverse effects was considered. Antibiotics and hydrocortisone were initiated, along with fluid resuscitation, and infectious workup was performed. After tapering hydrocortisone, the patient experienced transient hypotension and fever, which were managed with prednisone and sodium bicarbonate. Repeat blood work confirmed improved liver function and sodium bicarbonate levels.  

The patient is scheduled for outpatient follow-up with nephrology and oncology. She completed a prednisone taper over four weeks and denies symptoms at the follow-up. Discharge medications include sodium bicarbonate tablets.

The patient, a 39-year-old male, presented with low back pain, right hip pain, and bilateral foot pain, and developed enlarging soft masses in the plantar side of his right hallux. One year later, he was diagnosed with TIO (Type 2 Diabetes Insipothermia) with tumors in the right hallux. Initial lab results showed normal calcium levels, low phosphorus, and elevated alkaline phosphatase. Further testing confirmed elevated FGF23 levels, indicating overproduction of FGF23 due to TIO. Systemic venous sampling confirmed the diagnosis, and resection of tumors was performed. Histological examination showed oval-shaped mesenchymal cells with no mitotic activity or necrosis. Post-surgery, serum FGF23 decreased, and phosphorus levels returned to normal. The patient's pain resolved, and follow-up appointments are recommended.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information: Name: N/A; Age: 31; Gender: Female; Medical Record Number: N/A. Admitted to the department of neurosurgery at The First Hospital of Jilin University due to a right occipital mass for 5 months. Physical examination revealed a mass in the upper margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Head CT scan showed a 3×5 cm lesion composed of vascular components, described as a "wool mass." Further DSA examination confirmed an AVM and recommended surgical removal. The surgery was performed under general anesthesia, confirmed by postoperative pathology as IH accompanied by thrombolytic recanalization. The patient achieved a good recovery and was discharged. A head CTA review one year later showed partial residual IH without symptoms, and follow-up two years later showed no enlargement of the IH. The patient was recommended for radiation therapy for residual IH, but refused the therapy.

Discharge Summary:  
A 24-year-old woman was admitted on 09/30/2006 with muscle pain, myalgia, leukocytosis, neutrophilia, and monocytosis. Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), ESR, and creatine kinase (CK) were noted. She had fever and elevated CK, with a blood film showing atypical mononuclear cells. Midstream urine had a high white cell count. The patient was diagnosed with multifocal myonecrosis due to interstitial inflammation, consistent with CD4 lymphocytic infiltration. A right tibialis anterior muscle biopsy confirmed the findings. She was discharged on 10/04/2006 with a follow-up appointment and ongoing investigations. Discharge instructions include continuing medications, maintaining a healthy diet, attending follow-up with the primary physician, and reporting worsening symptoms.

The patient presented with shortness of breath, lower extremity edema, and flu-like symptoms. Initial treatment was for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), but further investigation identified a cardiac etiology. Diagnosis included a methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) infection, bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) with severe aortic regurgitation, and ascending aortic aneurysm. The patient underwent open-heart surgery with aortic valve replacement (AVR), ascending aortoplasty, and coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). Post-surgery, the patient had a good recovery with resolution of fever and bacteremia. He was discharged home on home health with antibiotics for eight weeks.

Discharge Summary:  
A 76-year-old male patient, admitted for an upper limb dissection, underwent an anomalous nerve branch dissection identified as a Kaplan anastomosis. The branch originated from the dorsal ulnar nerve, extending to include synovial membrane, abductor of the fifth finger, and skin of the area. It merged with the ulnar nerve trunk before bifurcating into superficial and deep rami. No further medical intervention was required, as the procedure was purely educational. The patient was discharged in good condition and advised to follow up with the primary care physician for future health concerns. Signed, [Doctor's Name], MD, PhD.

The patient, a 3-year-old male, was admitted to the emergency unit with a 4-day history of fever and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Initial diagnosis of Listeria monocytogenes meningitis was made, and intravenous amoxicillin and amikacin were initiated based on antibiotic susceptibility testing. Severe seizures were managed with phenobarbitone, which was successfully controlled. The patient was discharged after completing the 3-week antibiotic course and no fever or seizures were observed.  

Follow Up:

The patient completed protein-conjugated Pneumococcal and Haemophilus vaccines and was started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis to prevent recurrence. At the 6-month follow-up, the patient was walking normally with no neurologic deficits.  

Instructions:  
The family was instructed to monitor for any recurrence of bacterial meningitis and to seek medical attention promptly if new episodes occur.  

Final Diagnosis: Listeria monocytogenes meningitis

The 37-year-old Caucasian-Italian female patient, admitted in September 2006, was diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD), Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD), and Bulimic Disorder, according to DSM-IV criteria. She was treated with atypical antipsychotics, antidepressants, benzodiazepines, and psychotherapeutic interventions before being admitted. During her 24-month treatment, a combination of pharmacological therapy (aripiprazole and topiramate) and supportive psychotherapy led to significant improvements in mood, socio-relational functioning, and psychopathology. The patient demonstrated better emotional regulation, reduced impulsivity, and a greater degree of autonomy in her socio-relational life. She lost weight and discontinued hypoglycemic treatment, with antihypertensive therapy remaining unchanged. Discharge diagnosis included BPD, OCD, and Bulimia. Discharge instructions included continuing psychotherapy, maintaining a healthy diet, and adhering to dental hygiene guidelines.

Discharged on [date of discharge], patient died of sudden cardiac arrest 1 month post-chemotherapy and 5 months post-diagnosis of pancreatic metastases. Date: [date of discharge summary].

The patient was diagnosed with a nodular infiltrating papillary thyroid carcinoma, underwent a total thyroidectomy and adjuvant radioiodine therapy, and experienced recurrent papillary thyroid cancer with metastases. Due to the lack of second-line agents for metastatic papillary thyroid cancer, she was prescreened for the phase II basket study of entrectinib, which was enrolled and treated with entrectinib. The test revealed an EZR-ROS1 fusion, and the patient was enrolled and treated with entrectinib. During treatment, she experienced muscle weakness and difficulty with balance, requiring two dose reductions, but the lower dose therapy was well-tolerated. The patient is currently stable and will require ongoing monitoring and follow-up to assess long-term response and potential recurrence. Imaging showed a partial response by RECIST, with periaortic nodule and hypermetabolic liver metastasis resolved after 6 months. The patient's nontarget lesions in the left eighth rib and brain remain stable, and follow-up is planned.

A 45-year-old woman with a history of violaceous plaques on the forehead, chest, abdomen, back, and extremities, along with fever, weight loss, and general malaise was referred to the hospital for evaluation. She had been treated with topical steroids and phototherapy, but her condition worsened over time. Upon admission, she exhibited a 37.1°C body temperature, 5–10 mm violaceous plaques, and painful lymph nodes in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions. Her weight loss was 5 kg in a month.

A skin biopsy was performed, revealing infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells, and an immunohistochemical study confirmed no malignant lymphoma. The exact nature of the disorder is not yet determined. The patient was observed for a few days, and her condition responded to medication management and provided symptomatic relief. She was discharged and referred for follow-up with the dermatology department, advised to continue her prescribed medications and attend subsequent appointments, and to report new symptoms. The prognosis remains to be determined based on further diagnostic testing and clinical progress.

The patient, a 35-year-old male, was admitted with multiple injuries: a deep perforated wound in the right eye, a lacerated wound over the right hand, and abrasions over the right thigh. A CT scan was performed, revealing a right-sided globe rupture with profuse bleeding and a prolapsed, profusely bleeding ciliary body. Emergency evisceration was performed, and the patient remained stable post-op. He was discharged after 2 weeks with follow-up to monitor for recurrence or complications.

The patient, a 68-year-old man with a history of aortic insufficiency and ascending aort dilatation, was admitted to the emergency department with exertional dyspnea and coughing. A physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 100/50 mmHg and a heart rate of 80 beats/min, with normal sinus rhythm. A 3/6 diastolic decrescendo murmur was heard along the left sternal border, and a chest X-ray showed increased cardiothoracic index and prominent aortic arch. While awaiting laboratory results, the patient experienced severe chest pain, which was managed with an ECG showing ST segment elevation in aVR and diffuse ST segment depressions in all other leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe aortic regurgitation, a dilated ascending aorta with a diameter of 5.27 cm, and an intimal dissection flap that had prolapsed into the left ventricle during diastole. The left ventricular ejection fraction was within normal limits. The patient was immediately suggested surgery, but he suffered a sudden cardiopulmonary arrest and died after CPR.

A 53-year-old woman with a history of pulmonary emphysema and recurrent pneumothorax presented with fever, bilateral calf pain, and a cutaneous eruption over the lower extremities. She was treated for a pulmonary infection two weeks prior with Cefpodoxime. Admission blood tests revealed elevated C-reactive protein and ferritin levels, low albumin, and a positive Staphylococcus aureus sputum. A thoracic CT scan showed a right-sided apical lesion with mediastinal and hilar adenomegaly. Post-bronchoscopy sputum analysis confirmed Staphylococcus aureus infection. 

Diagnosis confirmed leukocytoclastic vasculitis (HSP) with immunoglobulin IgA staining and skin biopsy, consistent with HSP. A pulmonary aspiration smear was positive for acid-fast bacilli, and sputum culture yielded Mycobacterium xenopi. The patient was treated with Colchicin to manage pain and articular swelling, but developed severe abdominal pain and vomiting, prompting the initiation of intravenous methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day. Antibiotics and anti-mycotics were added, and follow-up imaging showed decreased pulmonary lesions. No recurrence of symptoms or complications was observed, with renal function preserved. The patient's condition improved, and no further treatment was required.

Patient: [redacted], 54 years, Female, admitted with a history of ventricular demand pacing (VVI) pacemaker implantation 22 years ago, with a right-sided lead removed and a new VVI pacemaker implanted 11 years ago. She was admitted with multiple vegetations on the pacemaker leads, septum, and tricuspid valve, and a fractured right-sided ventricular lead. Following lead removal, the left-sided lead was successfully removed, but the right-sided ventricular lead was left behind, resulting in a new vegetation on the newly implanted lead. The pacemaker was removed and replaced with a new one three months later, with a fever reported. TEE showed a new vegetation on the new lead. Open-heart surgery removed both vegetation and the lead, and an epicardial pacemaker was implanted. Discharge diagnosis: resolved vegetation on the new lead. No follow-up is recommended. Patient is stable and discharged.

64-year-old female cook presents with persistent numbness and burning sensation over the right anterolateral thigh for 2 months. She has a history of minor back trauma and well-controlled asthma with regular Seretide inhalers. Diagnosis is Meralgia paresthetica confirmed via MRI of the lumbosacral plexus, showing mild focal swelling in the right LFCN. Pregabalin 75-mg nocte and naproxen 275-mg twice daily were prescribed, but no relief was observed. Nerve conduction study showed no improvement, and the paraesthesia resolved completely spontaneously. Follow-up confirmed full recovery. The patient was diagnosed with meralgia paresthetica, and treatment was ineffective, but the condition resolved fully.
